Wildfire structure loss · outside the U.S.

Urban conflagrations outside the U.S. · 2026-10-15

417 fires in 10 countries (2016–2025) whose outline reached a block of at least 50 closely spaced buildings, chosen from open fire records without looking at losses, run through our Sentinel-2 damage model; 5 became urban conflagrations. Compared with the U.S. records, with a validation against Copernicus EMS gradings.

By Carlo Broderick, NCEAS, UC Santa Barbara · 2026-10-15 05:55 PDT

In the U.S. records, no fire whose biggest block of close buildings held 89 or fewer became an urban conflagration, and 10 of 25 above the line did. Outside the U.S., 0 of 178 fires at or below the line became one, and 5 of 239 above it (2%).C1: U.S. ours 0/701; abroad 0/178. C2: U.S. ours 10/25; abroad 5/239 (2%, exact 95% 1–5%; Fisher p vs ours 0.000). Outcome abroad = model calls (first call ≥ 0.88).

How to read this page

Urban conflagration: at least 50 destroyed buildings joined in one chain, each within 30 m (centre to centre) of another. Biggest block: the largest group of buildings of at least 50 m² inside the fire outline (plus 100 m), joined when their centres are within 35 m (about a 20 m gap between walls).

How this panel was checked
  • Same block rule (35 m links, buildings ≥ 50 m², outline + 100 m) and the same chain rule (30 m, ≥ 50) on both sides.
  • Different outcome source: U.S. = inspections / digitised losses; abroad = our first-call model on footprint maps. The U.S. like-for-like check below shows the damage call alone keeps 6 of 7 U.S. verdicts.
  • Fires below 50 abroad are counted from the block table and are 0 by construction (a 50-building chain cannot form).
  • Intervals are exact binomial ranges over fires; no bar is annualised or pooled across unlike periods.

Why the share above the line looks so low abroad

Check added after the results: U.S. chains seen through our model's miss rate

Abroad our model found about 43% of the buildings graded destroyed. Removing that many destroyed buildings at random from the U.S. records leaves about 0.5 of 10 urban conflagrations, about the share seen abroad. So the low share abroad can come from what the model misses, not from fewer real urban conflagrations.Post hoc (labelled; answers prereg amendment 2 item 3). p24 rows, our 2002–26 record, fires with b20 > 89; each destroyed counted building kept with probability r; 200 draws; LDC30 ≥ 50 recounted. Random thinning ignores spatial clustering of misses (whole neighbourhoods missing from a footprint map), so it is a rough guide.

How well the model works abroad

Building by building, against Copernicus EMS gradings

Abroad the model finds fewer of the destroyed buildings than in the U.S. and calls many more buildings destroyed that the gradings list as damaged or not listed at all. EMSR300 Rafina (Mati) 2018: 74 of 83 graded-damaged blocks that hold buildings from our list have at least one building we called destroyed, and 535 of 617 buildings we called destroyed lie inside graded-damaged blocks; EMSR715 Valparaíso 2024: 90 of 105 graded-damaged blocks that hold buildings from our list have at least one building we called destroyed, and 1,628 of 2,673 buildings we called destroyed lie inside graded-damaged blocks. Jasper 2024 (pilot, internal truth): recall 71%, precision 93%.One-to-one 10 m match (p14b convention), buildings ≥ 50 m²; EMS lists affected buildings only, so unlisted buildings in the area of interest count as not destroyed (precision is a lower bound). EMSR900/908 are 2026 events. Jasper from docs/ledger.d/2026-10-14-0215-intl-pilot-canada-mexico--result.md.

Independent test of a U.S. pattern: how the fire met the block

Vegetation on the approach side and slope into the block

In the U.S. the fires that became urban conflagrations reached their block across other built-up land more often than the near misses. This pattern was found after looking at the U.S. data; the fires abroad are its first independent test. What to keep in mind

Caveats

  • Building maps are made after the fire. Today's footprints miss destroyed buildings that were never rebuilt (Lytton, Tantallon, Denare Beach, Gyeongbuk villages show blocks under 50), and add later ones.
  • Building types differ. Masonry and concrete homes (Greece, Portugal, Spain, Turkey, Chile) and dense wooden villages (Japan, Korea) may burn and look different from U.S. wood-frame suburbs; the model was trained on U.S. fires.
  • Outlines differ. MODIS 500 m pixels (Chile, Korea, Japan) overstate what was reached; checks without them are in the table.
  • Not run: fires with no clear Sentinel-2 scene in the season (mostly Japanese winter fires), Fort McMurray 2016 and Funchal 2016 (before the scene archive used), NIAFED fires with no MODIS burn date.
  • A scientific estimate, not an official damage assessment.
